# Morocco TRAVEL SURVIVAL KIT

**Traveler Types Covered**: Budget/Luxury/Family/Solo

## 1. SIM CARD SOLUTIONS

**Purpose**: Obtain local mobile connectivity for calls, data, and internet access.

| **Provider** | **Price Options** | **Data Allocation** | **Validity** | **Where to Buy** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Maroc Telecom** | 50 MAD / 100 MAD | 5GB / 10GB | 7-30 Days | Airport kiosk, official stores |
| **Orange** | 49 MAD / 99 MAD | 5GB / 10GB | 15-30 Days | Main streets, airports |
| **Inwi** | 50 MAD / 100 MAD | 5GB / 12GB | 30 Days | Convenience stores, malls |
| **Airalo (eSIM)** | $9.50 USD | 2GB | 15 Days | Digital (App) |

- **Short trips**: Buy a physical SIM at the airport (often free SIM cards are handed out, you just pay for the top-up).
- **Best Coverage**: Maroc Telecom is the gold standard for desert excursions and mountain regions.

## 2. AIRPORT TRANSFERS

**Route**: From Casablanca Mohammed V (CMN) to Casablanca Center / Marrakech.

| **Mode** | **Duration** | **Cost** | **Booking** | **Best For** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **ONCF Train** | 35 mins (to Casa) | 50 MAD | Station counter | Speed, avoiding traffic |
| **Grand Taxi** | 45-60 mins | 300 MAD | Airport taxi rank | Door-to-door (groups) |
| **CTM Bus** | 1.5 hours | 20-30 MAD | Bus terminal | Budget solo travelers |
| **Private Transfer** | 3 hours (to Marrakech) | 1,200 MAD+ | Pre-booked online | Direct long-distance |

- **Details**: The train station is located at Level -1 in the arrivals area of Terminal 1. Grand Taxis have fixed prices posted on a board at the exit.

## 3. CURRENCY EXCHANGE

**Current Exchange Rate**: 1 USD ≈ 10.10 MAD (Moroccan Dirham)

| **Location** | **Why It's Best** | **Rates** | **Tips** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Hotel Ali (Marrakech)** | Legendary rates | Excellent | Located near Jemaa el-Fnaa |
| **Bureaux de Change** | Transparent | Good | Found in any "Ville Nouvelle" |
| **Al Barid Bank** | Reliable ATM | Mid-market | Best for international cards |

- **Universal Tips**: Avoid exchanging large amounts at the airport. Morocco is a cash-heavy society; always keep small denominations (10, 20 MAD) for tipping and markets.

## 4. MUST-HAVE APPS

| **App** | **Purpose** | **Key Features** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **InDrive** | Ride-hailing | Negotiate fare upfront (very popular in Morocco) |
| **Careem** | Ride-hailing | Fixed pricing for taxis/private cars |
| **Maps.me** | Navigation | Offline maps (essential for the winding medinas) |
| **ONCF Trafic** | Trains | Real-time schedules and ticket booking |
| **Glovo** | Food Delivery | Orders from local restaurants and pharmacies |

## 5. MUST-TRY FOODS

- 🍽️ **Tagine** – Slow-cooked stew in a clay pot. Try the Lamb with Prunes or Lemon Chicken.
- 🍽️ **Couscous** – Traditionally served on Fridays. Seven vegetables with steamed semolina.
- 🍽️ **Pastilla** – A sweet and savory pigeon or chicken pie with filo pastry and cinnamon.
- 🍽️ **Harira** – A hearty tomato, lentil, and chickpea soup used to break the fast.
- 🍽️ **Mint Tea** – Known as "Moroccan Whiskey." It is a symbol of hospitality.

## 6. UNIQUE ITEMS TO BUY

| **Item** | **Why Worth Buying** | **Where to Buy** | **Price Range** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Argan Oil** | Culinary or Cosmetic gold | Essaouira cooperatives | 100-300 MAD |

| **Leather Bags** | Traditional tanning | Fes Tanneries | 200-800 MAD |

## 7. SUPERMARKETS

- **Marjane**: The largest hypermarket chain; sells everything from electronics to alcohol (in separate sections).
- **Carrefour**: High-quality international goods and a reliable liquor store (Caves).
- **BIM**: Small, Turkish-owned convenience stores found in neighborhoods for basic snacks and water.

## 8. MARKETS (Day & Night)

| **Market Name** | **Location** | **Best For** | **Pro Tip** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Jemaa el-Fnaa** | Marrakech | Night food stalls | Eat at stall #14 or #1 |
| **Souk el Attarine** | Fes | Spices and scents | Get lost; it’s part of the fun |
| **Marche Central** | Casablanca | Fresh seafood | Buy fish and have it grilled nearby |

## 9. ALCOHOLIC DRINKS

| **Brand** | **Type** | **Profile** | **Price** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Casablanca** | Premium Lager | Crisp, refreshing | 30-60 MAD |
| **Flag Special** | Local Beer | Lighter, budget-friendly | 15-25 MAD |
| **Vin Gris** | Rose Wine | Unique Moroccan "Grey" wine | 80-150 MAD |
| **Mahia** | Spirit | Jewish-Moroccan fig brandy | 150 MAD+ |

- **Drinking Culture**: Alcohol is sold in licensed bars and specific supermarket "Caves." Public intoxication is highly frowned upon.

## 10. BEST PUBS & BARS

- **Le Grand Café de la Poste (Marrakech)**: Colonial-style elegance for a classic cocktail.
- **Sky 28 (Casablanca)**: Breathtaking views of the city from the Twin Center.
- **Café Baba (Tangier)**: A legendary, grit-meets-glam spot in the Kasbah once frequented by the Rolling Stones.

## BONUS SECTIONS

### 11. LOCAL FESTIVALS & EVENTS
Morocco hosts vibrant cultural events like the **Gnaoua World Music Festival** in Essaouira (June) and the **International Film Festival** in Marrakech (November). Religious holidays like **Ramadan** and **Eid** significantly alter business hours and atmosphere.

### 12. CUSTOMS & ETIQUETTE

#### 12a. Temple & Sacred Site Dress Code
Mosques in Morocco (except Hassan II in Casablanca) are generally closed to non-Muslims. Modesty is expected at all religious landmarks.

| **Rule** | **What to Check** | **Enforcement Level** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Shoulders/Knees** | Cover both regardless of gender | Strict at Hassan II |
| **Footwear** | Remove shoes at the entrance | Mandatory |
| **Head covering** | Generally not required for tourists | Respected |

#### 12b. The Head, Feet & Body — Cultural Hierarchy
The right hand is used for eating and greeting, as the left is traditionally for hygiene. 

- **The Right Hand**: Always use your right hand to eat from communal tagines and to shake hands.
- **Modesty**: In rural areas, exposing too much skin is considered disrespectful.

#### 12c. Religious Interactions & Etiquette
Respect the call to prayer (Adhan) five times a day.

| **Rule** | **Detail** | **Who It Applies To** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Prayer Time** | Avoid loud music or disruptions | All visitors |
| **Photography** | Ask before filming people praying | All visitors |
| **Mosque Entry** | Do not enter if non-Muslim | Strictly enforced |

#### 12d. Saving Face & Conflict Resolution
Moroccans value hospitality and politeness; public anger is seen as a loss of dignity. Always haggle with a smile—it is a social game, not a battle.

#### 12e. Responsible Tourism & Child Welfare
Avoid giving money to children begging in the streets to prevent school truancy. Support local artisans directly and choose eco-friendly desert camps that respect water scarcity.

#### 12f. General Social Customs & Greetings
Greetings are often lengthy; a hand over the heart after a handshake shows sincerity. Tipping (Baksheesh) is a standard part of the economy for almost every service.

### 13. SAFETY & PRACTICAL INFORMATION

#### 13a. Vaccinations & Preventative Health
Consult a doctor 6 weeks before travel.

| **Vaccine** | **Priority** | **Notes** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Hepatitis A** | Recommended | Food/water safety |
| **Typhoid** | Recommended | For adventurous eaters |
| **Tetanus** | Recommended | Standard booster |

#### 13b. Mosquito-Borne Illness & Insect Protection
Malaria risk is negligible, but Leishmaniasis exists in some rural areas.

| **Disease** | **Peak Risk** | **Prevention** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Leishmaniasis** | Rural/Night | DEET and covered skin |

#### 13c. Water & Food Safety
Tap water is generally chlorinated in cities but can cause upset stomachs for visitors.

| **Source** | **Safety** | **Guidance** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Tap Water** | Caution | Stick to bottled water |
| **Ice** | Moderate | Avoid in street stalls |

#### 13d. Personal Safety & Crime Awareness
Morocco is generally safe for tourists, but petty crime and specific scams are common in high-traffic areas.

- **ISSUE**: Petty Theft & Bag Snatching
- **WHERE IT HAPPENS**: Crowded souks, Jemaa el-Fnaa, and busy medina alleys.
- **HOW IT HAPPENS**: Distraction techniques or quick snatches in narrow streets where motorbikes can pass.
- **HOW TO AVOID IT**: Wear backpacks on your front in crowds. Use a cross-body bag and keep it zipped. Avoid wearing expensive jewelry.
- **WHAT TO DO IF IT HAPPENS**: Report immediately to the "Brigade Touristique" (Tourist Police), who are very protective of the tourism industry.

- **ISSUE**: "Faux Guides" (False Guides)
- **WHERE IT HAPPENS**: Entrances to Medinas (Fes and Marrakech specifically).
- **HOW IT HAPPENS**: Locals (often young men) will tell you a street is "closed" or a monument is "shut for prayer," then offer to lead you elsewhere, eventually demanding a high fee or leading you to a family shop.
- **HOW TO AVOID IT**: Politely say "No thank you" or "I know the way." Use GPS/Maps.me. If you are truly lost, ask a shopkeeper or a woman with children for directions instead of someone hovering on the street.

- **ISSUE**: Henna and Animal Scams
- **WHERE IT HAPPENS**: Jemaa el-Fnaa square.
- **HOW IT HAPPENS**: Women may grab your hand and start a "free" henna design, then demand 200+ MAD. Similarly, men may place a monkey or snake on your shoulders for a photo and demand payment.
- **HOW TO AVOID IT**: Keep your hands to yourself and walk with purpose. Firmly say "No" before they start. If they persist, walk away immediately.

#### 13e. Emergency Contacts
Always keep these numbers saved in your phone.

| **Service** | **Contact** | **Notes** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Police (Cities)** | 19 | Standard emergency |
| **Gendarmerie (Rural)** | 177 | Outside major cities |
| **Ambulance/Fire** | 15 | Medical emergencies |
| **Tourist Police** | +212 524 384 601 | (Marrakech branch) |

### 14. SEASONAL CONSIDERATIONS
- **Summer (June-Aug)**: Intense heat in the interior (Marrakech/Fes can hit 45°C).
- **Winter (Dec-Feb)**: Cold nights in the desert and Atlas mountains; snow is common.
- **Ramadan**: Dates change annually; many cafes are closed during daylight hours.
